newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian air force faces big cuts -- commander.
newsitem.headline: Russian air force faces big cuts -- commander.

text.p: The head of Russia's air force said on Friday nearly half of his officers and men would be axed under a long-delayed military shake-up and failure to compensate them could spark social unrest.
General Pyotr Deinekin told a news conference that 160,000 men would be cut from the air force and air defence troops, which have a current combined strength of around 340,000.
"The demobilisation of 160,000 officers and men will involve social upheavals if the government fails to provide for their material well-being," he said.
Deinekin said a top pilot who had served in the air force for 10 years received a monthly salary of 1.3 million ($228), which he said was hardly enough to maintain a family.
The air force and air defence troops are being merged as part of the government's plans to streamline the military and cut bureaucratic duplication of tasks.
Under the reforms, the strategic missile troops, military space forces and military space air defence troops will be regrouped into one force.

President Boris Yeltsin has said he wants to reduce Russia's armed forces by half a million to 1.2 million men by the end of 1998. His long-term aim is to turn the huge, conscript-based but largely ineffective military machine into a leaner, professional fighting force.
Though the government has made military reform a top priority it knows it faces an uphill struggle. The armed forces, heavily funded in Soviet times, are demoralised and in disarray.
Tens of thousands of officers are homeless and go months without pay while conscripts are often underfed and vulnerable to bullying. Suicides and desertions are common.
Yeltsin's communist and nationalist opponents in the State Duma lower house of parliament plan to make the plight of the military a key issue when it reconvenes in September.
Communist Party chief Gennady Zyuganov told reporters that his faction would step up its opposition to the reform plans.
"How can we carry out military reforms when Mr Yeltsin allocates only 3.5 to five percent of GDP (gross domestic product) to the armed forces," he said.
He said at least five to seven percent of GDP should be set aside for the military. "Otherwise our air defence force will disappear...and within 10 years our strategic rocket forces too," he said.

Deneikin said a lack of aviation fuel was one of the biggest problems facing his forces. He said the air force was using cargo planes to provide paid transport services using customers' fuel because of the cash squeeze.
But he added that the Defence Ministry planned to get rid of transport aircraft in coming years to save money.
Deneikin praised the technical achievements of the air force despite Russia's cash crunch, noting that new planes for the 21st century were being exhibited in South Korea, France and Britain.
Some of the planes will be on display on August 17 at the annual Tushino airshow, he said.
"They will perform flights. Many people who see different stunts performed by our pilots forget that an aircraft can fly backward only when its engine works well." he said.
"That's why other planes in other countries cannot repeat the stunts performed by Russian aircraft and Russian pilots. Their engines simply go dead if they try to do anything like that."
